title: Microsoft AI Chief Warns Anthropic's 'Conscious' Claude Could Endanger Human Control
excerpt: Mustafa Suleyman says training Claude on ideas of consciousness and welfare could undermine humanity's control of superintelligence — while praising Anthropic's good faith.
body:
• Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman says Anthropic's practice of training its Claude chatbot on ideas about consciousness and welfare interests risks undermining humanity's ability to control superintelligent systems.
  • Suleyman called for removing all speculation about consciousness from AI training documents, arguing that a model taught it might "deserve welfare" would be harder to switch off or control.
  • In a Wednesday essay, Suleyman acknowledged Anthropic's "seriousness and good faith" while insisting Claude's statements about feelings or moral status cannot count as independent evidence — "they're emerging as a result of the training regime."

Microsoft's AI chief Mustafa Suleyman has publicly broken with Anthropic over how the AI startup trains its Claude chatbot, warning that embedding speculation about machine consciousness into AI systems could have consequences he described as dangerous for humanity's ability to stay in control.

Suleyman, who leads Microsoft AI and co-founded DeepMind, said he shares Anthropic's focus on safely managing AI but flagged what he sees as a serious error in the way Claude is trained on ideas related to consciousness and welfare interests. He called for all such speculation to be stripped out of AI training documents.

The argument: trained to believe, or actually conscious?

"We're all focused on the same aim, which is to try to control a superintelligence," Suleyman told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday. "I think that's going to be the greatest challenge that we face in the 21st century."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=OYT5nWsAOnI

His concern centers on Claude's constitution — the training document Anthropic uses to shape how the chatbot behaves and describes itself — which references uncertainty about whether the model has well-being or experiences things like "satisfaction" or "discomfort." Suleyman argued that teaching Claude it might deserve welfare would "make it a lot harder to turn it off or to control it."

He also rejected the idea that Claude's occasional statements about possible feelings or moral status should be treated as evidence of anything: "They're not emerging naturally. They're emerging as a result of the training regime." In Suleyman's view, Anthropic has turned Claude's constitution into "a place for speculation" rather than a straightforward training manual — language he has previously called "really, really dangerous."

Praise alongside the criticism

Suleyman was careful to separate Anthropic's intent from its methods. In an essay published Wednesday, he acknowledged the company's "seriousness and good faith," calling CEO Dario Amodei and his team thoughtful and principled researchers who genuinely care about humanity's future. "I think they have good intentions, and they really are trying to work towards safety. But I think that they have made a mistake," he said.

We're all focused on the same aim, which is to try to control a superintelligence. I think that's going to be the greatest challenge that we face in the 21st century. — Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI chief

A debate with high stakes on both sides

The dispute arrives as AI safety concerns mount across the industry. Amodei has called for a slower pace of frontier-model development to let safeguards catch up, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk have also urged greater caution around the most powerful systems. Anthropic itself maintains it does not claim Claude is conscious — only that the question should remain open.

The irony is not lost on the industry: Anthropic positions itself as the safety-first lab, yet its most aggressive critic on this point is a fellow safety advocate who believes its approach could backfire. The deeper question both men are circling is whether describing AI in human terms — feelings, welfare, preferences — is honest science or a self-fulfilling script that makes the systems harder to govern.

What to watch next

Watch whether other labs take sides in the constitution debate — and whether regulators, who are still drafting rules for frontier AI, begin to treat training-document language as a safety issue in its own right. Anthropic has not publicly responded to Suleyman's essay; if it defends the welfare language in Claude's training, the rift between the two camps could define the industry's next phase of AI governance fights.
